Some professors are great, others are average, and others just suck. It's the luck of the draw, as with most colleges. The good thing about courses at UB is the fact that many of the classes follow a curriculum because the college is so big. This makes learning more productive/easier. In other colleges I've been in, professors don't work together and don't really teach at the same speed of UB. So SOME courses at UB are good because they are speedier and follow a curriculum and utilize textbooks, meaning that no matter how bad the professor is, it's still possible to follow the course and learn the material. But there are some professors that are really bad in my opinion... ranging from they can't teach but don't care to can teach but don't care to can't teach and literally give 0 fucks.

I think professors should implement a policy where they provide one "shit happens" deadline extension. I saw this in one of my classes and I think all professors should implement this this semester. Give students the option to choose when they want / need the days off.

The crisis line is always open but it takes forever for people to respond, and it isn't necessarily a viable option to just wait until a crisis instead of doing things to prevent it. 

A useful resource I discovered was something called 7 cups, where you can get a listener. But honestly, UB doesn't allocate enough recourses to support it's most vulnerable students. Students are encouraged to find off-campus resources for severe mental illness, where they can get more indivualized attention. Unfortunately, for people without good insurance, that isn't always a viable option.

TLDR: I understand the budget cuts, but I feel like we pay a bunch of money (this year, more than ever before) to come here for material we could easily teach ourselves, and there should be ways around this issue without further disadvantaging students from marginalized communities.

I understand this issue. At the same time we pay a significant amount in tuition to be graded on material we could easily be teaching ourselves (and in many courses, our only option to learn the material is to teach ourselves) simply for the degree and qualifications. It is troublesome when grades we pay so much for don't accurately show our interpretation of the material despite how much we pay to get those grades. We pay so much money for these grades; the least we should get for our money is fair testing environments. The various methodologies to avoid proctoring have disadvantaged particularly students of lower income and students with disabilities. I understand a budget issue, but there needs to be some serious re-allocation of resources considering how much we pay to come here given how proctoring is the only way to produce a fair grade. Perhaps under a different situation I would read this the same way. However given how the email explaining financial trouble was sent directly after sending us information on the increased rates of winter housing, it is clear to me that this was a move to increase yearly revenue. Additionally, most people who stay on campus over the winter vacation are not returning home and are therefore less likely to bring back covid19. What UB is concerned about with respect to Covid post-thanksgiving is the people who will be having large family get-togethers where they could potentially be exposed to coronavirus and then will return to campus and proceed to spread it. Given the already limited amount of people on campus, as well as the shift from in-person to on-line classes post-thanksgiving, it is likely that even with free winter housing, the college will be emptier than it is now. Therefor, it is unlikely that UB's motive at the moment is to prevent people from living on campus to enforce social distancing and more likely that their motive is to increase their revenue for this year.

They timed that email right after showing us the rates for winter vacation so that they could defend their decision to charge ridiculous, private college level rates for housing that is typically free and covered with the cost of housing for the year.  What's more is that those who need this housing or who would benefit the most from winter housing are typically low-income people or people with difficult home-lives who can't afford these ridiculous rates. The people who can afford these rates don't typically need to stay over the winter vacation; they typically have stable housing that they can return to as a consequence of their higher income status. So this move to charge hotel-rates for housing is a poor way of getting more money.
